claims.text: The material family of interest is multiphase alloys with chemical-ordering tendencies.
These alloys will exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during aging.
Sequential formation and dissolution of ordered precipitates cause the non-monotonic ductility transition.
Ordered precipitates alternately impede and facilitate dislocation motion as aging proceeds.
The as-quenched initial state is a supersaturated solid solution.
The as-quenched initial state has no long-range chemical order.
Isothermal aging below the solvus can induce precipitation in the target alloy.
Short-range order evolves into long-range-ordered precipitates during aging.
Further aging causes the ordered precipitates to coarsen or dissolve into a disordered matrix.
SRO/LRO formation creates strong anti-phase-boundary barriers.
Strong anti-phase-boundary barriers cause an intermediate brittle state.
Precipitate coarsening or transformation to a disordered structure reduces anti-phase-boundary barriers.
Reduction of anti-phase-boundary barriers restores ductility at longer aging times.
Ductility versus aging time will follow a U-shaped or V-shaped curve.
The ductility minimum will coincide with the peak density or strength of the ordered precipitates.
The transition requires an aging regime that permits formation of a metastable ordered phase that becomes unstable at longer times or higher temperatures.
The transition requires a matrix that remains sufficiently ductile in both the initial and final states.
The hypothesis is falsified by a monotonic ductility curve or by failure of the ductility minimum to correlate temporally with peak ordered-phase density or strength.
